Five plants that separate a designed garden from a planted one. Rosemary — most people treat it as a herb. Designers use it as a structural evergreen with silver foliage, late winter bloom, and serious drought tolerance once established. Echinops — steel-blue globe thistle that holds its form into winter. Pollinators love it, it seeds around just enough, and nothing else gives you that texture. White Cloud Nepeta — all the soft billowing habit of catmint, none of the blue. Cleaner in a white or silver palette. Underused because most people don’t know it exists. Mountain Hydrangea (Hydrangea serrata) — more refined than arborescens, lacecap form, better fall color, and it actually performs in part shade without flopping. Blue Mist Fothergilla (Fothergilla gardenii ‘Blue Mist’) — blue-green foliage all season, then flame in fall. Native, compact, and genuinely beautiful. The plant that makes clients ask “what is that?” #gardendesign #landscapedesign

Most landscaping owners do not own a business. They own a job that does not stop when they do. There's a book called The E-Myth by Michael Gerber every operator should read. Most small businesses struggle because the owner is a technician — great at the work — who assumes being good at the work means they can run the business. Those are two different things. The technician does it himself, until there's more work than one person can do. Then he's buried, working in the business every hour, with no time to work on it. Gerber's test: could you hand this business to someone else and would it keep running the way you built it? If not, you don't own a company. You own a job, and you're the only employee who can't quit. Stop working in the business long enough to build the business. #commerciallandscaping #landscapingbusiness #leadership #businessowner #emyth

Every grade, surface, and transition needs to be carefully prepared before the next step begins. Taking the time to prepare the site correctly helps prevent uneven areas and creates the clean, polished finish you see in the final landscape.
